title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person under sentence or lawfully committed
bareActText: Whoever, being a public servant, legally bound as such public servant to apprehend or to keep in confinement any person under sentence of a Court for any offence or lawfully committed to custody, intentionally omits to apprehend such person, or intentionally suffers such person to escape or intentionally aids such person in escaping or attempting to escape from such confinement, shall be punished,— (a) with imprisonment for life or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to fourteen years, with or without fine, if the person in confinement, or who ought to have been apprehended, is under sentence of death; or (b) with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, with or without fine, if the person in confinement or who ought to have been apprehended, is subject, by a sentence of a Court, or by virtue of a commutation of such sentence, to imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term of ten years, or upwards; or (c) with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both, if the person in confinement or who ought to have been apprehended, is subject by a sentence of a Court to imprisonment for a term not extending to ten years or if the person was lawfully committed to custody.
plainMeaning: The same wrong as s.259, but where the person is already under a court's sentence, or lawfully committed to custody — so the punishment is heavier. A public servant legally bound to arrest or keep confined such a person, who intentionally fails to arrest him, lets him escape, or helps him escape, is punishable: with life imprisonment or up to fourteen years if the person is under sentence of death; up to seven years if he is serving life or ten years or more (including by commutation); and up to three years, or fine, or both, if he is serving less than ten years or was lawfully committed to custody.
ingredients: The accused is a public servant legally bound to apprehend, or keep in confinement, a person under sentence of a Court or lawfully committed to custody
He intentionally omits to apprehend the person, or intentionally suffers him to escape, or intentionally aids his escape or attempted escape
Punishment depends on the sentence the person is under
punishment: (a) Person under sentence of death: imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description up to 14 years, with or without fine. (b) Person sentenced to life or 10 years or more: up to 7 years, with or without fine. (c) Person sentenced to less than 10 years, or lawfully committed to custody: up to 3 years, or fine, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: (a) Court of Session; (b), (c) Magistrate of the first class

title: Escape from confinement or custody negligently suffered by public servant
bareActText: Whoever, being a public servant legally bound as such public servant to keep in confinement any person charged with or convicted of any offence or lawfully committed to custody, negligently suffers such person to escape from confinement, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
plainMeaning: Sections 259 and 260 require intention; s.261 covers carelessness. A public servant legally bound to keep in confinement a person charged with or convicted of an offence, or lawfully committed to custody, who negligently lets him escape, is punishable with simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.
ingredients: The accused is a public servant legally bound to keep in confinement a person charged with or convicted of an offence, or lawfully committed to custody
The person escapes from confinement
The accused negligently suffered the escape
punishment: Simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacted without change of substance or punishment.

illustrations: A constable guarding an arrested accused in hospital falls asleep on duty with the ward door open, and the accused walks out. The constable negligently suffered the escape and is liable under s.261.

title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension
bareActText: Whoever intentionally offers any resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of himself for any offence with which he is charged or of which he has been convicted, or escapes or attempts to escape from any custody in which he is lawfully detained for any such offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.—The punishment in this section is in addition to the punishment for which the person to be apprehended or detained in custody was liable for the offence with which he was charged, or of which he was convicted.
plainMeaning: A person who intentionally resists or illegally obstructs his own lawful arrest for an offence he is charged with or convicted of, or who escapes or tries to escape from lawful custody for such an offence, is punishable with up to two years, or fine, or both. Under the Explanation, this punishment is in addition to any punishment for the original offence.
ingredients: Lawful apprehension of the accused for an offence he is charged with or convicted of; or his lawful custody for such an offence
He intentionally resists or illegally obstructs the apprehension; or escapes or attempts to escape from the custody
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both — in addition to the punishment for the original offence.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacted without change of substance or punishment, with its Explanation.

illustrations: When police arrive with a warrant to arrest Z for cheating, Z locks himself in and then climbs out of a back window to flee. Z is liable under s.262, in addition to any sentence for cheating.

title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person
bareActText: Whoever, intentionally offers any resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of any other person for an offence, or rescues or attempts to rescue any other person from any custody in which that person is lawfully detained for an offence,— (a) shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both; or (b) if the person to be apprehended, or the person rescued or attempted to be rescued, is charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine; or (c) if the person to be apprehended or rescued, or attempted to be rescued, is charged with or liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with death, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; or (d) if the person to be apprehended or rescued, or attempted to be rescued, is liable under the sentence of a Court or by virtue of a commutation of such a sentence, to imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term of ten years or upwards, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine; or (e) if the person to be apprehended or rescued, or attempted to be rescued, is under sentence of death, shall be punished with imprisonment for life or imprisonment of either description for a term not exceeding ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.
plainMeaning: A person who intentionally resists or illegally obstructs the lawful arrest of someone else for an offence, or rescues or tries to rescue someone from lawful custody for an offence, commits this offence. The punishment rises with the gravity of the other person's situation: (a) up to two years, or fine, or both, as the basic offence; (b) up to three years and fine if the person is charged with an offence punishable with life or up to ten years; (c) up to seven years and fine if charged with an offence punishable with death; (d) up to seven years and fine if he is serving a sentence of life or ten years or more; and (e) life imprisonment or up to ten years and fine if he is under sentence of death.
ingredients: Lawful apprehension of another person for an offence, or that person's lawful custody for an offence
The accused intentionally resists or illegally obstructs the apprehension; or rescues or attempts to rescue the person from custody
Punishment depends on what the other person is charged with or sentenced to
punishment: (a) Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both. (b) Charged with an offence punishable with life or up to 10 years: up to 3 years, and fine. (c) Charged with an offence punishable with death: up to 7 years, and fine. (d) Under sentence of life or 10 years or more: up to 7 years, and fine. (e) Under sentence of death: imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description up to 10 years, and fine.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: (a) Any Magistrate; (b)-(d) Magistrate of the first class; (e) Court of Session

title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not otherwise provided for
bareActText: Whoever, being a public servant legally bound as such public servant to apprehend, or to keep in confinement, any person in any case not provided for in section 259, section 260 or section 261, or in any other law for the time being in force, omits to apprehend that person or suffers him to escape from confinement, shall be punished— (a) if he does so intentionally, with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both; and (b) if he does so negligently, with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
plainMeaning: A residuary provision filling gaps left by ss.259-261. A public servant legally bound to arrest or keep confined any person, in a case not covered by those sections or by any other law, who fails to arrest him or lets him escape, is punishable: up to three years, or fine, or both, if he does so intentionally; and simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, if negligently. It would apply, for instance, to a person detained under a civil process or for reasons other than an offence.
ingredients: The accused is a public servant legally bound to apprehend, or keep in confinement, a person
The case is not provided for in ss.259, 260 or 261 or any other law
He omits to apprehend the person, or suffers him to escape
(a) Intentionally or (b) negligently
punishment: (a) Intentional: imprisonment of either description up to 3 years, or fine, or both. (b) Negligent: simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: (a) Magistrate of the first class; (b) Any Magistrate

title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise provided for
bareActText: Whoever, in any case not provided for in section 262 or section 263 or in any other law for the time being in force, intentionally offers any resistance or illegal obstruction to the lawful apprehension of himself or of any other person, or escapes or attempts to escape from any custody in which he is lawfully detained, or rescues or attempts to rescue any other person from any custody in which that person is lawfully detained, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine, or with both.
plainMeaning: The residuary counterpart of ss.262-263. In any case not covered by those sections or another law — typically where the arrest or custody is not for an offence (for example, civil arrest) — a person who intentionally resists or illegally obstructs the lawful arrest of himself or another, escapes or tries to escape from lawful custody, or rescues or tries to rescue another from lawful custody, is punishable with up to six months, or fine, or both.
ingredients: A case not provided for in ss.262 or 263 or any other law

Intentionally resisting or illegally obstructing the lawful apprehension of oneself or another; or escaping or attempting to escape from lawful custody; or rescuing or attempting to rescue another from lawful custody
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 6 months, or fine, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacted without change of substance or punishment.

illustrations: In the example under s.264, if the judgment-debtor had instead pushed the bailiff away and run off, he would be liable under s.265, since the arrest was not for an offence.

title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment
bareActText: Whoever, having accepted any conditional remission of punishment, knowingly violates any condition on which such remission was granted, shall be punished with the punishment to which he was originally sentenced, if he has already suffered no part of that punishment, and if he has suffered any part of that punishment, then with so much of that punishment as he has not already suffered.
plainMeaning: The Government can remit (reduce or cancel) a sentence on conditions — for example, early release on condition of good behaviour or reporting to the police. A person who has accepted such a conditional remission and knowingly breaks any of its conditions is punished with his original sentence if he had served none of it, or with the unexpired remainder if he had served part. It is cognizable and non-bailable, and triable by the court that could try the original offence.
ingredients: The accused accepted a conditional remission of punishment
He knowingly violates a condition on which the remission was granted
punishment: The original sentence, if no part has been served; otherwise the part not yet served.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: The Court by which the original offence was triable

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacted without change of substance. The IPC's s.226 (unlawful return from transportation) had already been repealed and has no BNS equivalent.

illustrations: A convict serving seven years is released after four years on remission, on condition that he does not leave the district without police permission. He knowingly moves to another State. He is liable to serve the remaining three years under s.266.

title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding
bareActText: Whoever, intentionally offers any insult, or causes any interruption to any public servant, while such public servant is sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding, shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.
plainMeaning: A person who intentionally insults, or causes any interruption to, a public servant while he is sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding — most often a judge or magistrate in court — is punishable with simple imprisonment up to six months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both. The court can deal with it summarily under BNSS Chapter XXVIII when committed in its view or presence. It sits alongside the separate power of courts to punish contempt under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971.
ingredients: The victim is a public servant sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding
The accused offers an insult to him, or causes an interruption
He does so intentionally
While the public servant is so sitting
punishment: Simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)
classification.triableBy: The Court in which the offence is committed, subject to Chapter XXVIII of the BNSS; or, if not committed in a Court, any Magistrate

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacts s.228 IPC. The IPC's s.228A (disclosure of identity of a rape victim) is not in this Chapter; the BNS deals with it in s.72.

illustrations: Angry at an adjournment, a litigant stands up in court and shouts abuse at the magistrate, stopping the proceedings. He is liable under s.267.

title: Personation of assessor
bareActText: Whoever, by personation or otherwise, shall intentionally cause, or knowingly suffer himself to be returned, empanelled or sworn as an assessor in any case in which he knows that he is not entitled by law to be so returned, empanelled or sworn, or knowing himself to have been so returned, empanelled or sworn contrary to law, shall voluntarily serve as such assessor, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.
plainMeaning: Assessors were lay persons who sat with a judge to help decide a case. A person who, by personation or otherwise, intentionally causes himself (or knowingly allows himself) to be returned, empanelled or sworn as an assessor when he knows he is not legally entitled to be, or who voluntarily serves as an assessor knowing that he was so appointed contrary to law, is punishable with up to two years, or fine, or both. The BNS covers assessors only; the IPC's corresponding provision also referred to jurors.
ingredients: By personation or otherwise, intentionally causing or knowingly suffering oneself to be returned, empanelled or sworn as an assessor, knowing one is not legally entitled; or
Knowing one was so returned, empanelled or sworn contrary to law, voluntarily serving as such assessor
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or fine, or both.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacts s.229 IPC, which covered 'personation of a juror or assessor'; the BNS refers only to assessors.

illustrations: A man answers to another person's name when the list of assessors is called in a trial, and is sworn in as that person. He is liable under s.268.

title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court
bareActText: Whoever, having been charged with an offence and released on bail bond or on bond, fails without sufficient cause (the burden of proving which shall lie upon him), to appear in Court in accordance with the terms of the bail or bond, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. Explanation.—The punishment under this section is— (a) in addition to the punishment to which the offender would be liable on a conviction for the offence with which he has been charged; and (b) without prejudice to the power of the Court to order forfeiture of the bond.
plainMeaning: A person charged with an offence and released on a bail bond or bond who fails to appear in court as the bail or bond requires, without sufficient cause, is punishable with up to one year, or fine, or both. The burden of proving sufficient cause is on him. Under the Explanation, this punishment is in addition to any sentence for the original offence, and does not affect the court's power to forfeit the bond. It is cognizable and non-bailable.
ingredients: The accused was charged with an offence
He was released on bail bond or bond
He failed to appear in Court in accordance with its terms
Without sufficient cause — which he must prove
punishment: Imprisonment of either description up to 1 year, or fine, or both — in addition to the punishment for the original offence, and without prejudice to forfeiture of the bond.

classification.compoundable: Not compoundable (not listed in BNSS s.359)

ipcReference.changeNote: Re-enacts s.229A IPC; the BNS wording refers to a 'bail bond or bond'.

illustrations: Released on bail in a theft case on condition that he attends every hearing, A skips three hearings to attend a family wedding abroad, without the court's permission. Unless he proves sufficient cause, A is liable under s.269, in addition to any sentence for theft, and the court may also forfeit his bail bond.
